comment: Editorial seeds. Each takes a slot on its date before anything scored, and the generator fills the rest. See docs/DAILY_FACTS.md. `article` is the source and headline subject; `imageArticle` overrides only where the picture comes from.

facts.title: Wikipedia opens
facts.body: An encyclopedia anyone could edit went live, as a side project meant to feed articles to a more serious one written by experts. The serious one closed in 2009.
facts.alt: An early screenshot of the Wikipedia main page.

facts.title: The first telephone call
facts.body: Alexander Graham Bell made the first successful telephone call, to his assistant in the next room: "Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you."
facts.alt: A portrait photograph of Alexander Graham Bell.

facts.title: Me at the zoo
facts.body: YouTube co-founder Jawed Karim posted nineteen seconds of himself standing in front of the elephants at San Diego Zoo. It was the first video ever uploaded to the site.
facts.alt: A photograph of YouTube co-founder Jawed Karim.

facts.title: Deep Blue beats Kasparov
facts.body: A chess computer won a full match against a reigning world champion for the first time. Kasparov, convinced no machine could have played that well, accused IBM of hiding a human.
facts.alt: A photograph of the Deep Blue chess computer.

facts.title: The Antikythera mechanism
facts.body: A Greek archaeologist noticed that a corroded lump raised from a shipwreck was full of gear teeth. It is a two-thousand-year-old machine for predicting eclipses.
facts.alt: The largest surviving fragment of the corroded Antikythera mechanism.

facts.title: Harambe
facts.body: A gorilla at Cincinnati Zoo was shot after a three-year-old boy climbed into his enclosure. The argument about whether it was necessary turned into a meme that outlasted the news by years.
facts.alt: A western lowland gorilla, the subspecies Harambe belonged to.

facts.title: The iPhone goes on sale
facts.body: People queued outside Apple stores for days for a phone that could not send a picture message, record video, or run any software but Apple's own. The app store was a year away.
facts.alt: Steve Jobs presenting the original iPhone on stage.

facts.title: MTV signs on
facts.body: The channel opened with "Video Killed the Radio Star" by The Buggles. Hardly anyone saw it: MTV was not carried in New York or Los Angeles, so the launch party watched on a feed from New Jersey.
facts.alt: The MTV logo used by the music television channel.

facts.title: The first computer bug
facts.body: Operators found a moth stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark II. They taped it into the logbook and wrote underneath it: "First actual case of bug being found."
facts.alt: A page from a computer logbook, illustrating the history of software bugs.

facts.title: The first :-)
facts.body: Scott Fahlman suggested :-) and :-( on a Carnegie Mellon message board, so people could tell which posts were jokes. The original message was lost for twenty years, then found on a backup tape.
facts.alt: A smiley face, the symbol the first emoticon was drawn to represent.

facts.title: The first message online
facts.body: The first computer-to-computer message was sent from Los Angeles to Stanford over ARPANET. It was meant to say LOGIN. The system crashed after LO.
facts.alt: A logical map of the early ARPANET computer network.

facts.title: The Berlin Wall opens
facts.body: An East German spokesman, misreading a note at a press conference, said the border was open immediately. Crowds went to the checkpoints to find out, and the guards let them through.
facts.alt: Crowds of West and East Germans at the Brandenburg Gate in 1989.

facts.title: The first text message
facts.body: An engineer typed "Merry Christmas" on a computer and sent it to a colleague's phone. Phones of the day could receive a text message but had no way to write one back.
facts.alt: A mobile phone showing a received text message.

facts.title: The Mother of All Demos
facts.body: Douglas Engelbart spent ninety minutes demonstrating the computer mouse, hypertext links, video calling and two people editing one document at once. Most of it took another twenty-five years to arrive.
facts.alt: Douglas Engelbart during his 1968 computing demonstration.
